analysis.one_liner: Extends family leave and equal-treatment protections to part-time and temporary workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 and referred to four House committees; with no hearing or vote scheduled and 34 of 217 House Democrats signed on, it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change two things about being a part-time worker. First, it would open unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave (FMLA) to anyone who has been on the job 90 days, replacing the current rule that requires 12 months of service and at least 1,250 hours in the past year — a bar that screens out most part-timers. Second, it would make it illegal for employers with more than 15 employees to pay part-timers less, deny them benefits, or pass them over for promotions just because they work fewer hours, and it would require employers to offer extra hours to existing workers — at least at the hours and times those workers said they wanted — before hiring anyone new, including through temp agencies. Workers could sue for lost pay plus equal damages, and the Labor Department could investigate and fine employers who retaliate. The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers — a group concentrated in retail, food service, caregiving, and gig-adjacent jobs, and disproportionately women — gain access to job-protected family and medical leave, pro-rata benefits, preferred hours before new hires, and legal recourse when employers pay or schedule them differently because of their hours. Workers at franchised chains and staffing-agency placements are covered because the bill counts whole franchise networks and integrated enterprises toward the 15-employee threshold [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It rewrites the Family and Medical Leave Act so a worker qualifies for unpaid, job-protected leave after 90 days on the job, instead of after 12 months and at least 1,250 hours — the threshold that screens out most part-timers.

It bars employers with more than 15 employees from paying part-timers less, denying them pro-rata paid time off, or passing them over for promotion merely because they work fewer hours than comparable full-time staff.

It obliges employers to record each worker's desired weekly hours and availability, to offer open hours to existing staff before hiring outsiders or temps, and to pay existing staff for hours that go instead to a new hire during a time the worker said they were available.
It gives workers enforcement teeth: lawsuits for lost wages plus equal liquidated damages, attorney's fees, and Labor Department investigations and civil penalties for willful retaliation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with more than 15 employees who rely heavily on part-time and temporary staff — retailers, restaurants, hotels, and staffing agencies — bear new costs: pro-rata benefits for part-timers, scheduling constraints from the hours-preference rules, record-keeping, and damages plus attorney's fees when workers win suits [S2]. Some of that cost may reach consumers through prices or show up as fewer part-time openings [S2].

drawbacks.text: Retailers, restaurants, and other large part-time employers would face new costs: paid time off and benefits accrue pro rata for part-timers, extra hours must be offered to current staff before new hires, and records of hour offers must be kept for at least three years.

The scheduling provisions could cut against the workers they aim to help: because employers must pay existing staff for hours that go to new hires, and must honor written availability statements, some employers may hire fewer part-time workers or tighten the hours they offer at the start.

Counting franchised chains and integrated enterprises in the aggregate toward the 15-employee threshold would bring many individually small franchise locations under the law and expose the networks to shared liability.

Opening FMLA to all employees past 90 days removes the experience-based limit, so covered employers could see more leave taken by newer, lower-tenure staff, with attendant scheduling and coverage costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For part-time workers the gains are concrete: family and medical leave after 90 days, pro-rata benefits, a claim on extra hours before outsiders are hired, and pay damages when employers skirt the rules [S2]. The costs fall on large part-time employers — retailers, restaurants, franchised chains, and staffing agencies — in the form of benefit expenses, scheduling constraints, record-keeping, and lawsuit exposure [S2]. An honest supporter should acknowledge that some of those costs could come back as fewer part-time openings or higher prices; the bill's exceptions for qualifications, availability, and overtime are designed to limit that, but they cannot eliminate it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, and with no hearing or vote scheduled since, it is sitting in committee.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on December 17, 2025, with 33 Democratic cosponsors joining sponsor Janice Schakowsky.
The same day, it was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee and, in addition, to the Committees on House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record after the referral.
All 34 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: large part-time employers avoid the new requirements while the bill sits without a hearing, and part-time workers gain nothing yet.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, in a House where Republicans hold 223 of 441 seats — so the bill currently has no path to a floor vote without Democratic-only unity and majority cooperation.

industries.note: These are the largest employers of part-time and variable-hour staff, so the pro-rata benefits rule, the hours-preference rule, and the pay remedy hit their labor model and scheduling practices directly. Their flexibility savings come out of part-timers' pay and benefits.

The bill blocks employers from turning to temps or contractors before offering the hours to existing employees who asked for them, shrinking the temp-placement market this industry depends on. Cheaper flexible labor for employers is what temp staffing sells, at the cost of steady hours for the workers inside it.

Franchise networks are counted in the aggregate toward the 15-employee threshold, so individually small franchise locations would be covered and franchisor networks could face shared liability. The aggregation rule targets exactly the structure used to keep each unit below coverage thresholds.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has only Democratic cosponsors in a Republican-held House and was referred to four committees, which multiplies the hurdles — any one chair can keep it from a markup, and none has scheduled one. Bills at this stage with no hearing in their first months typically die quietly when the Congress ends. Unless Democrats take the House in 2026 or the bill picks up Republican cosponsors, its realistic path is no further action.
